body:
## Resolution
`_dfm_selfdir` was `dirname "$0"` with no symlink resolution. Invoked via a prior
install's `~/.local/bin/dfm` symlink, `$0` is the symlink path, so `_dfm_selfdir` became
`~/.local/bin` — which need not contain newly added dfm-* siblings (or even dfm-lib) until
`./install` links them, and with the repo's local/bin absent from $PATH the dispatcher failed
to load dfm-lib at all (died at the N-133 guard) and could not find new subcommands. This made
developing a new `dfm-<sub>` require a re-link first. Fixed by resolving `$0` through its
symlink chain (portable `readlink` loop, no `-f`, with `cd -P`) so `_dfm_selfdir` is the
script's REAL directory (the repo's local/bin), keeping the script's own folder authoritative
ahead of $PATH. Verified: a fresh repo-only `dfm-zzdemo`, never linked and with repo/local/bin
off $PATH, runs via a symlinked `dfm zzdemo`; `dfm help`/`check arch` via symlink still work;
43/43 bats pass; `yarn lint` clean.

body:
## Resolution
After the dfm command split, the dispatcher's `$PATH` fallback was
`if command -v "dfm-$sub"; then exec "dfm-$sub"`. bash's `command -v` returns a
non-executable file when it is first on `$PATH`, and `$DOTFILES/local/bin` (which holds the
0644 `dfm-lib`) is on `$PATH` via `config/exports:25`. So `dfm lib` resolved `dfm-lib` and
exec-ed it → "Permission denied", nonzero exit — defeating the design property that the
non-executable dfm-lib is undispatchable. Fixed by resolving the path and guarding the exec
with `-x`: `resolved=$(command -v "dfm-$sub"); [[ -n "$resolved" && -x "$resolved" ]] && exec`.
Verified: `dfm lib` now falls through to usage, exit 0, no "Permission denied".

popup (`prefix + t` via `tmux display-popup -E`,
`config/tmux/tmux.conf:96`) and `fzf-tmux -p` cannot open a second
popup. The cascade was reverted and an explanatory comment block was
added at the top of `sesh.sh` documenting the popup-nesting
constraint.

body:
## Problem

Six command substitutions in the test suite use the BSD-first fallback
`$(stat -f FMT FILE 2>/dev/null || stat -c FMT FILE)`. On GNU coreutils,
`stat -f` means "filesystem status", so the BSD format string is parsed
as a *file operand*: stat errors on `%Lp`/`%m` (exit 1, triggering the
fallback) but **still prints a multi-line filesystem-status block for the
real file to stdout**. The substitution captures that block plus the
fallback's value, so the compared string is never `600`/`700`/a bare
mtime.

Sites: `tests/dfm.bats:319,478,495,497` and `tests/theme-lib.bats:47,50`.

## Evidence

`bats tests/` at HEAD on Linux 6.8: 4 failures —
`not ok 31 dfm secrets create writes files readable only by owner`
(`[ "$perms" = "600" ]` failed), `not ok 48 ... directories owner-only`
(`[ "$perms" = "700" ]` failed), the re-tighten test at dfm.bats:499
(`[ "$fperms" = "600" ]` failed), and theme-lib.bats:51
(`[ "$before" = "$after" ]` failed — the captured blocks embed live
`Free:` block counts that change between the two calls).

Empirical demo on this host:
`perms="$(stat -f '%Lp' f 2>/dev/null || stat -c '%a' f)"` yields
`File: "..." / ID: ... / Block size: 4096 / ... / 600` (262 bytes of
filesystem status + the real value).

The production code under test is correct: `local/bin/dfm-lib:243-265`
sets umask 077 and explicitly chmods 700/600.

## Impact

The suite (`test-all.sh`, the package.json test script) is
deterministically red on every Linux host, and the failing assertions are
exactly the ones verifying the security-critical secrets-permission
behavior — a real permission regression on Linux would be
indistinguishable from the known-red state.

## Fix

Swap each substitution to GNU-first; BSD stat rejects `-c` with an error
on stderr and no stdout, so the ordering is safe on macOS:
`perms="$(stat -c '%a' FILE 2>/dev/null || stat -f '%Lp' FILE)"`
(and `stat -c %Y ... 2>/dev/null || stat -f %m ...` in theme-lib.bats).
This mirrors the already-correct probe pattern in
`local/bin/tv-gh-repos:86-95` (`cache_file_mtime`).

## Resolution
Swapped all six substitutions GNU-first (stat -c ... || stat -f ...) in tests/dfm.bats and tests/theme-lib.bats; full suite 189/189 green on Linux 6.8.
title: BSD-first stat fallback breaks 4 bats tests on GNU/Linux

body:
## Problem

`config/fish/conf.d/theme-switch.fish:35,46` capture the mode-file mtime
with the BSD-first fallback
`(stat -f %m $mode_file 2>/dev/null; or stat -c %Y $mode_file 2>/dev/null)`.
On GNU/Linux, `stat -f %m FILE` exits 1 (so `or` runs the fallback) but
first prints a multi-line filesystem-status block for `$mode_file` to
stdout. The captured variable is therefore a multi-element fish list:
filesystem-status lines (including live `Free:` block counts) plus the
real mtime.

## Evidence

Empirically verified on this host (Linux 6.8, GNU coreutils):
`stat -f %m FILE 2>/dev/null` → exit 1, 262 bytes of filesystem status on
stdout. The same defect makes `tests/theme-lib.bats:51` fail, proving the
`Free:` counts change between two captures ~1s apart.

The per-prompt watcher at line 46 compares
`test "$__theme_switch_last_mtime" != "$mtime"`; both sides embed
free-block counts, so any disk write between two prompts makes the
strings differ even though the mode file's mtime is unchanged.

## Impact

On Linux, the "cheap watcher" trips its expensive branch on effectively
every prompt after any disk activity: `echo y | fish_config theme save
"Catppuccin Mocha"` (subprocess + theme-file write), ls-colors re-read,
and BAT_THEME reset run per prompt instead of only on real theme flips.
Adds per-prompt latency and constant writes to fish's theme file.

## Fix

Swap both substitutions to GNU-first (BSD stat rejects `-c` cleanly with
no stdout):
`(stat -c %Y $mode_file 2>/dev/null; or stat -f %m $mode_file 2>/dev/null)`
at lines 35 and 46.

## Resolution
GNU-first stat order in theme-switch.fish lines 35/46; fish -n and fish_indent --check pass.
title: theme-switch.fish mtime capture polluted on Linux; watcher trips every prompt

## Problem

The context-mode sandbox tools (`ctx_execute`, `ctx_execute_file`,
`ctx_batch_execute`) execute arbitrary code with full write access to the
working tree, bypassing the entire file-protection hook chain:
`pre-edit-block.sh` matches only `Edit|Write|Read|MultiEdit`, and the
PostToolUse format/validate hooks likewise never fire for sandbox-side
writes. `.claude/rules/bash-routing.md` declares
"`ctx_execute`/`ctx_execute_file` to write files — use `Write`/`Edit`" a
forbidden pattern, but nothing enforces it.

## Evidence

Verified in this session: a Python `open(path, 'w')` inside `ctx_execute`
created a file in the repo tree (removed immediately after), and
`open('local/bin/fzf-tmux', 'r+')` — a file `pre-edit-block.sh` exists to
protect — succeeded. Settings matcher dump:
`Edit|Write|Read|MultiEdit -> pre-edit-block.sh`, `Bash ->
pre-bash-route.sh`; no matcher covers any `mcp__plugin_context-mode_*`
tool.

## Impact

An agent (or a prompt-injected instruction) can modify hook-protected
paths — `local/bin/fzf-tmux`, `yarn.lock`, `.yarn/`, submodule paths,
real `secrets.d` files — and land unformatted/unvalidated edits, without
any deny, warning, or auto-format firing. The written rule exists; the
enforcement surface has a hole the project's own routing rules actively
push traffic toward.

## Fix

Add a PreToolUse hook entry matching the context-mode execute tools
(matcher `mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute|...ctx_execute_file|...ctx_batch_execute`)
that scans the `code`/`commands` input for write patterns targeting
protected paths (the same list `pre-edit-block.sh` guards) and denies
with the pre-edit-block message. Coarse but sufficient: the protected-path
list is short and literal; matching the path strings in the submitted
code catches the realistic bypass shapes.

## Resolution
Added .claude/hooks/pre-ctx-write-guard.sh + PreToolUse matcher for the three ctx execute tools; five self-test payloads behave correctly (deny writes to protected paths and secrets reads, pass benign/example/null-redirect).
title: context-mode sandbox writes bypass pre-edit-block and all post-edit hooks

## Problem

On a remote (SSH) host, opening a new tmux window flips the theme to dark
even when the user's terminal is in light mode. Three defects cooperate:

1. `config/theme/probe-osc11` emits a bare `\033]11;?\007`. Inside a tmux
   pane that query is intercepted by tmux itself instead of the outer
   terminal, despite `allow-passthrough on` in `config/tmux/tmux.conf:19`
   existing exactly for this — the probe never uses the passthrough
   envelope, so tmux answers with its own (dark/absent) background or not
   at all.
2. The SSH branches of the shell bootstrap treat a failed probe as
   `dark` and run `apply dark` (`config/exports:493-496`,
   `config/fish/config.fish:90-96`), overwriting the correct `light`
   state file written moments earlier by the pre-tmux login shell.
3. The probe's 0.2s default timeout ignores SSH round-trip latency, and
   `read -d $'\007' ... || exit 0` discards ST-terminated replies
   (`\e\\`) that were fully parseable from the partial read.

## Evidence

- `config/theme/probe-osc11:40` — `printf '\033]11;?\007'` unwrapped.
- `config/theme/probe-osc11:44` — `read -t 0.2 -d $'\007' ... || exit 0`.
- `config/exports:494` — `[ "$m" = dark ] || [ "$m" = light ] || m="dark"`.
- `config/fish/config.fish:91` — `test "$m" = dark -o "$m" = light; or set m dark`.
- Failure scenario: ssh into host (login shell probes real terminal ->
  light written to state), attach tmux, open new window -> probe inside
  pane gets no/false answer -> `apply dark` fires all handlers -> whole
  session turns dark.

## Impact

Every new tmux window (or pane shell) on an SSH host resets the entire
remote theme (tmux, starship, fish colours, LS_COLORS, bat) to dark,
making light mode unusable over SSH inside tmux.

## Fix

- probe-osc11: wrap the query in the tmux passthrough envelope when
  `$TMUX` is set; default timeout 1s when `SSH_TTY`/`SSH_CONNECTION` is
  set (0.2s otherwise, `--timeout` still wins); replace `|| exit 0` on
  the read with `|| true` so ST-terminated/partial replies still parse.
- exports + config.fish SSH branches: on probe failure fall back to the
  cached state (`theme_mode`/`theme-mode`, which itself defaults dark)
  instead of hard `dark`, so a silent probe never clobbers known state.
- Add a bats case for ST-terminated replies.

## Resolution
probe-osc11 now wraps OSC 11 in the tmux passthrough envelope, uses a 1s default timeout over SSH, and parses ST-terminated partial replies; exports/config.fish SSH branches fall back to cached state instead of hard dark. Regression test added (ST-terminated reply); theme bats suite 29/29, pre-commit clean.
title: SSH tmux theme probe answered by tmux and hard dark fallback clobbers light state

## Problem

The repo's error-reporting helper prints errors on stdout. Diagnostics are therefore indistinguishable from data, and the sibling helper in `config/lib.sh` does the opposite.

## Evidence

Measured directly:
- `msgr err "ERRMSG" 1>/dev/null` prints nothing — the message was on stdout.
- `msgr err "ERRMSG" 2>/dev/null` prints the message — confirming stdout.
- `msgr warn "WARNMSG" 1>/dev/null` prints nothing — same for warnings.
`grep -rl 'msgr err' local/bin scripts config` matches 21 files.
By contrast `config/lib.sh` documents `logger::error` as writing timestamped output to stderr, so the two helpers in the same repo disagree.

## Failure scenario

Any caller whose stdout is data: `x-env-list > vars.txt` on an error path writes the error marker into vars.txt and shows the user a clean terminal. Any caller that logs with `cmd >> run.log 2>&1` cannot separate diagnostics from output, and `cmd 2>&1 >/dev/null` — the usual idiom for keeping only errors — discards exactly the errors.

## Impact

Errors are silently swallowed or silently injected into data, across 21 files. `msgr err` also exits 0, so a caller cannot fall back on the exit code either.

## Fix

Redirect inside the helpers only — `msg_err` and `msg_warn` gain `>&2` on their printf. Callers need no change. Verify with the two probes above, then re-run `bats tests/` for the scripts that assert msgr output.

## Note

Found while writing tests for msgr, after the apply-fixes prompt. Not fixed: moving a stream is a behaviour change across 21 callers and was not in the approved fix set.

## Resolution
msg_err and msg_warn now write to stderr. Verified: 2>&1 1>/dev/null shows them, 2>/dev/null hides them, ok still on stdout, and $(msgr err ...) captures nothing. No caller captured msgr output, so no call site needed changing.
title: msgr err and msgr warn write to stdout, so errors vanish from logs and corrupt captured output

`yarn lint` is the repo's quality gate — run by the Stop hook, referenced throughout CLAUDE.md — but four of the binaries it invokes are declared nowhere.

`package.json` has no `dependencies` and no `devDependencies` key at all; its top-level keys are name, version, description, directories, scripts, repository, keywords, author, license, bugs, homepage, resolutions, packageManager.

Declare the four in `config/mise/config.toml` alongside biome and editorconfig-checker (mise has npm backends: `"npm:prettier"`, `"npm:markdownlint-cli"`, `"npm:v8r"`, `"npm:markdown-table-formatter"`), or add them as devDependencies and invoke them through yarn. Once declared, `mise install && yarn lint` is a runnable CI step.

## Resolution
Wrong: all four ARE declared, at config/mise/config.toml:96-99 as npm:-prefixed keys. My grep anchored on ^prettier and "prettier and missed the "npm: prefix. The real and narrower gap - those pins live only in the global mise config, which a CI checkout never reads - was folded into the CI fix by adding the lint toolchain to the repo-root .mise.toml.

Added a lint job to tests.yml (which triggers on push), using jdx/mise-action pinned to 9e7f7633 v4.2.3, plus corepack enable and yarn lint. ## Problem

Every interactive shell pays close to a second of startup. For a dotfiles repo this is the primary user-facing performance metric, and nothing in the repo measures or budgets it.

## Evidence

Measured on this machine, 3 runs each of `<shell> -i -c exit`, wall time divided by 3:
- zsh 820ms
- bash 536ms
- fish 418ms
The shared chain is `config/shared.sh` -> `config/lib.sh` + `config/exports` + `config/alias`. `config/exports` runs `mise activate` and `brew shellenv` on every start; zsh additionally loads antidote plugins; all three render a starship prompt and the theme watcher is spawned from shell init.

## Impact

820ms is perceptible on every new pane, every `tmux split-window`, and every shell a script spawns interactively. The theme popup bound to `<prefix> m` pays it too, since `display-popup -E` starts a login shell.

## Profile (measured, not guessed)

`zsh -c 'zmodload zsh/zprof; source ~/.zshrc; zprof'`, function self-time:

| Function              | Time  | Share |
|-----------------------|-------|-------|
| `fzf_setup_using_fzf` | 138ms | 55%   |
| `_mise_hook`          | 66ms  | 26%   |
| `use-omz.zsh` anon    | 12ms  | 5%    |
| `normalize_path_var`  | 12ms  | 5%    |

The components suspected in the original write-up are not the cost: `mise activate zsh` is 20ms, `starship init zsh` 3ms, `zoxide init zsh` 2ms, `fzf --zsh` 3ms. `brew` is not installed on this host, so the `brew shellenv` guess did not apply at all.

## Partially fixed

Two duplicated-work defects found by the profile are fixed: `compinit` ran twice per start (`base/zshrc` called it explicitly while the ez-compinit plugin, loaded via antidote, already had — and honours the same `$ZSH_COMPDUMP`), costing 37ms of compinit plus 17ms of compaudit. Removing the duplicate took zsh from **820ms to 681ms** over 5 runs, with completions verified intact (`_comps` = 1753, `compdef` and `complete` both defined).

## Fix

Two of the four profile entries are already dealt with (see "Partially fixed"). What remains needs a decision rather than an edit — see "Remaining" for why each is not mechanical, and pick one:

1. Defer the fzf integration behind a lazy widget so the 138ms is paid on first use rather than every start. Accepts a delay before fzf keybindings become live.
2. Switch `mise activate` to `--shims` to drop the 66ms hook, accepting slower per-command shim resolution and different version-switch behaviour.
3. Accept 681ms and add a bats startup-time assertion so it does not regress further.

## Remaining

`fzf_setup_using_fzf` at 138ms is now 55% of the profile, and it lives in `config/fzf/key-bindings.zsh` / `completion.zsh` — vendored files that `.claude/rules/vendored-files.md` forbids editing. Reducing it means deferring the fzf integration behind a lazy widget rather than modifying it, which changes when keybindings become live and needs a deliberate decision. `_mise_hook` at 66ms is inherent to `mise activate`; the alternative is `mise activate --shims`, which trades hook cost for shim-resolution cost and changes behaviour for version switching.

Neither is a mechanical fix, so both are left for a decision rather than applied. Once a budget is agreed, add a startup-time assertion to the bats suite so regressions surface.

## Resolution
zsh 820ms -> 470ms (5-run average, same method throughout). Three duplicated-work defects removed: OMZ's fzf plugin (138ms, 55% of the profile) which duplicated source_fzf_config's vendored setup; a second compinit call (37ms + 17ms compaudit) already performed by ez-compinit on the same dumpfile; and two startup errors filed separately. fzf verified intact after removal: fzf-history-widget, fzf-file-widget, fzf-cd-widget all defined, ^R and ^T still bound, _fzf_complete present. Remaining top cost is _mise_hook at 58ms, inherent to mise activate. Not done: no startup-time budget or bats assertion exists, so nothing prevents regression.
title: Interactive shell startup is 418-820ms; zsh is the worst at 820ms

## Problem

Line 106 carries a `# nosec B603` suppression for a check that does not trigger there. Bandit reports the stale suppression explicitly on every run, so the repo's new bandit gate emits warning noise on an otherwise clean pass.

## Evidence

The line:

```python
git_dir = check_output(["git", "rev-parse", "--git-dir"]).decode("utf-8").strip()  # nosec B603 # nosemgrep
```

Bandit's response, on a clean (exit 0) run:

```
$ bandit -c pyproject.toml -r . -q
[tester]	WARNING	nosec encountered (B603), but no failed test on file ./local/bin/x-git-largest-files.py:106
[tester]	WARNING	nosec encountered (B603), but no failed test on file ./local/bin/x-git-largest-files.py:106
```

The other six `# nosec B603` comments in the file (lines 111, 119, 159, 160, 190) suppress real findings — bandit's summary counts `Total potential issues skipped due to specifically being disabled (e.g., #nosec BXXX): 8`.

## Impact

Two warning lines print on every `yarn lint` and every pre-commit run, on a pass. Warning output that always appears trains the reader to skip it, which is how the next real warning gets missed. The `# nosemgrep` half of the same comment is still load-bearing (Opengrep/Semgrep flags `dangerous-subprocess-use-audit` on `check_output`), so the whole comment cannot simply be deleted.

## Fix

Drop only the bandit half of the suppression, keeping the semgrep half:

```python
git_dir = check_output(["git", "rev-parse", "--git-dir"]).decode("utf-8").strip()  # nosemgrep
```

Then confirm the warnings are gone and the gate still passes:

```
bandit -c pyproject.toml -r . -q; echo "rc=$?"
```

Expect no `[tester] WARNING` lines and `rc=0`.

## Resolution
Premise disproved by removing the suppression. The finding claimed `# nosec B603` at x-git-largest-files.py:106 was dead because bandit prints "nosec encountered (B603), but no failed test on file ./local/bin/x-git-largest-files.py:106". Deleting the `# nosec B603` half made B603 fire at exactly that location: "[B603:subprocess_without_shell_equals_true] ... Location: ./local/bin/x-git-largest-files.py:106:14", Low severity / High confidence, and the gate went from rc=0 to rc=1 with the skipped-issue count dropping 8 -> 7. The suppression is load-bearing and has been restored verbatim. The warning is a bandit reporting quirk on check_output (it emits the notice twice per run, before the test verdict is attached), not evidence of a stale nosec. No code change warranted.
title: Dead `# nosec B603` suppression on a line where B603 never fires

## Problem

`.claude/rules/vendored-files.md` opens with "Three trees are vendored in-tree" and lists fzf, the graphify skill, and the iTerm2 integration. It presents itself as authoritative, and `.claude/hooks/pre-edit-block.sh` implements exactly that list. But five more files under `config/fish/functions/` are third-party code refreshed from upstream, and none of them appear in either the rule or the hook.

## Evidence

Upstream provenance, from the file headers:

- `config/fish/functions/fisher.fish:3` — `set --local fisher_version 4.4.8` (jorgebucaran/fisher)
- `config/fish/functions/bass.fish` + `config/fish/functions/__bass.py:1-7` — docstring "To be used with a companion fish function like this: ... /tmp/bass.py source" (edc/bass)
- `config/fish/functions/__z_add.fish:1` — `function __z_add -d "Add PATH to .z file"` (z for fish)
- `config/fish/functions/__z_clean.fish:1` — `function __z_clean -d "Clean up .z file to remove paths no longer valid"`

`.claude/hooks/pre-edit-block.sh` case list covers `*/fzf-tmux`, `*/config/fzf/…`, `*/.claude/skills/graphify/*`, `*/iterm2_shell_integration.zsh`, `*/tools/{dotbot,dotbot-include,antidote}/*`, `*/config/cheat/cheatsheets/{community,tldr}/*`, `*/secrets.d/*.fish`. There is no arm matching `config/fish/functions/`.

## Impact

An agent asked to "fix the bug in fisher.fish" edits it with no block and no warning — the rule that would have stopped it does not name the file. The edit survives review because it looks like ordinary project code, then is silently discarded the next time the plugin is refreshed from upstream. This is the exact failure mode `vendored-files.md` exists to prevent; it just has an incomplete inventory. `__bass.py` also accounts for 5 of the repo's 23 Codacy issues (B404, 2x B603, 2x Opengrep dangerous-subprocess-use), all unactionable for the same reason.

## Fix

Add a fourth section to `.claude/rules/vendored-files.md` naming the five files with their upstreams and refresh procedure, correct the "Three trees" sentence, and add a matching arm to `.claude/hooks/pre-edit-block.sh`:

```bash
  */config/fish/functions/fisher.fish | */config/fish/functions/bass.fish | \
    */config/fish/functions/__bass.py | */config/fish/functions/__z_add.fish | \
    */config/fish/functions/__z_clean.fish)
    echo "BLOCKED: $fp is a vendored fish helper — refresh from upstream." >&2
    echo "See .claude/rules/vendored-files.md." >&2
    exit 2
    ;;
```

`.codacy.yml` and `[tool.bandit] exclude_dirs` in `pyproject.toml` already exclude these paths as of this run, so the scanner half is done; the rule and hook halves are not.

## Resolution
Both halves closed. `.claude/rules/vendored-files.md`: corrected "Three trees" to "Four groups", added the five files to the frontmatter `paths:` list, and added a "fish plugin functions" section with an upstream table (fisher, bass/__bass.py, __z_add, __z_clean), the fisher_version:4.4.8 marker to check on refresh, and a note that the scanner exclusions already exist in pyproject.toml and .codacy.yml. `.claude/hooks/pre-edit-block.sh`: added a case arm matching all five paths. Verified by feeding the hook a real payload — an Edit to config/fish/functions/fisher.fish exits 2 with the BLOCKED message, an Edit to a hand-written sibling (mkcd.fish) exits 0. `bash -n` and shellcheck both clean on the hook.
title: Five vendored fish helpers are undeclared and unprotected by the vendored-files guard

`.claude/rules/bash-routing.md:20`:

```
- `pre-commit run`, `yarn lint`, `yarn test`, `yarn check` — every quality gate
```

The full script list in `package.json` is:
`fix, fix:biome, fix:md-table, fix:prettier, format, format:yaml, lint, lint:bandit, lint:biome, lint:ec, lint:markdownlint, lint:md-table, lint:prettier, lint:usage, lint:v8r, test`

## Problem

`.yarnrc.yml` combines an unrestricted git-dependency allowlist, enabled install scripts, and a 3-day publish-age gate. Each is defensible alone; together, on a repo whose dependency PRs are opened and landed by a bot, they leave no meaningful window in which a compromised release would be caught before it executes code on the machine.

## Evidence

Full contents of `.yarnrc.yml` (104 bytes):

```yaml
---
approvedGitRepositories:
  - "**"
enableScripts: true
nodeLinker: node-modules
npmMinimalAgeGate: 3
```

Semgrep's `package_managers.yarn.yarn-missing-minimal-age-gate` rule flags line 6 at MEDIUM: "This .yarnrc.yml does not set a minimal age gate or sets it too low. Newly published packages can be malicious or unstable. Add `npmMinimalAgeGate: \"7d\"`".

The repository's recent history is dominated by bot-authored dependency commits — the last analysed commit on `main` is `e1836f1 chore(deps): update pre-commit hook gitleaks/gitleaks (v8.30.0 -> v8.30.1) (#604)`, authored by `renovate[bot]`, and the four commits before it are also renovate bumps (#601-#605).

## Impact

`enableScripts: true` means a package's `postinstall` runs arbitrary code at `yarn install` time — including inside the Stop-gate hook, which calls `yarn install --no-immutable` before linting. `approvedGitRepositories: ["**"]` removes the confirmation step for any git-hosted dependency. `npmMinimalAgeGate: 3` shortens the quarantine to three days; the documented typosquat/compromise pattern is detected and yanked within roughly a week, which is why the rule's threshold is 7d. A malicious release published on day 0 is installable on day 3, lands via an automated bump PR, and executes its install script on the next lint run.

## Fix

Raise the gate to the rule's threshold and narrow the git allowlist to the repos actually depended on:

```yaml
npmMinimalAgeGate: "7d"
```

If no dependency is git-hosted (nothing in `package.json` uses a git specifier), delete the `approvedGitRepositories` key entirely rather than leaving `"**"`; if some are, list them explicitly. Leave `enableScripts: true` only if a dependency demonstrably needs it — check with `yarn install --mode=skip-build` first; if the install succeeds, set `enableScripts: false` and re-enable per package via `dependenciesMeta.<pkg>.built`.

## Resolution
All three axes closed, and the investigation found the gate was worse than filed. `yarn config get npmMinimalAgeGate` now reads 10080 (minutes = 7 days) for the new value "1w"; the previous bare `3` therefore meant 3 MINUTES, not 3 days, so the age gate was effectively absent rather than merely short. `enableScripts` set to false (Yarn's own documented default — the repo had explicitly opted in, and the Stop-gate hook runs `yarn install --no-immutable` every turn, so a postinstall would have run unattended). `approvedGitRepositories` narrowed from ["**"] to [] — the repo declares zero dependencies (no dependencies/devDependencies block, 2-entry yarn.lock, no git resolutions, empty node_modules), so nothing legitimate is blocked and a future git dep now requires this file to change in the same commit. Verified live: `yarn install --no-immutable` rc=0, config readback 10080/false/[], and `yarn dlx <email> moo` still rc=0, so the dlx workflow documented in docs/commands.md:56 is unaffected.
title: Yarn supply-chain settings are permissive on all three axes while renovate auto-lands dependency bumps

## Problem

Ruff formats Python code blocks embedded in Markdown, and one such block in `.claude/rules/read-routing.md` is unformatted. The repo has ruff wired into pre-commit, but the `ruff-format` hook only receives Python-typed files, so the failure is invisible to every configured gate.

## Evidence

```
$ ruff format --check .claude/rules/read-routing.md
unformatted: File would be reformatted
  --> .claude/rules/read-routing.md:60:1
   |
59 | import re
60 +
61 | with open("config/homebrew/Brewfile") as f:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
71 | import re
72 +
73 | with open("config/mise/config.toml") as f:
   |

1 file would be reformatted
```

Repo-wide, `ruff format --check .` reports `1 file would be reformatted, 136 files already formatted`.

The pre-commit hook that would catch it does not see the file — `.pre-commit-config.yaml` declares `ruff-format` with only an `exclude:` for the completions directories, so it inherits the upstream hook's `types_or: [python, pyi, jupyter]`. Markdown never matches. `yarn lint` does not invoke ruff at all: the chain is `lint:biome && lint:prettier && lint:ec && lint:md-table && lint:markdownlint && lint:v8r && lint:usage && lint:bandit`.

## Impact

Small in itself — one blank line in a documentation snippet. It matters because it is a silent gate hole rather than an accepted exception: anyone who runs the obvious repo-wide command gets a failure that neither pre-commit nor CI would have reported, and the natural reading of that is "the gates are broken" rather than "this file is out of scope". The same hole hides any future unformatted Python snippet in any Markdown file, and this repo's rule files are dense with them.

## Fix

Fix the file, then close the hole. The formatting fix is to delete the stray blank line ruff wants removed at `.claude/rules/read-routing.md:60` and `:72` — run `ruff format .claude/rules/read-routing.md`.

To gate it, add `types_or` to the existing hook in `.pre-commit-config.yaml` so Markdown is included:

```yaml
      - id: ruff-format
        types_or: [python, pyi, jupyter, markdown]
        exclude: ^config/(bash/completions\.d|zsh/completions\.d)/
```

Alternatively, if Markdown snippets should stay out of scope deliberately, say so in `pyproject.toml` under `[tool.ruff.format]` via `exclude = ["*.md"]` — an explicit exclusion beats an accidental one.

## Resolution
Fixed the file and closed the gate hole. Added the blank line after `import re` that ruff wanted in both Python snippets in .claude/rules/read-routing.md (ruff was requesting an addition, not a deletion). `ruff format --check .` now reports "144 files already formatted", rc=0, and `ruff check .` passes. Added `types_or: [python, pyi, jupyter, markdown]` to the ruff-format hook in .pre-commit-config.yaml so Markdown is no longer invisible to the gate — previously the hook inherited the upstream types_or and never saw a .md file, which is why the failure could exist while every configured gate reported clean.
title: `ruff format --check .` fails on a rule file and no gate in the repo catches it

## Problem

`tests/x-macos.bats` calls `run` with a flag argument but never declares the bats version that makes flags meaningful. On bats older than 1.5.0 the flag is treated as the command to run rather than as an option, so the test asserts something other than what it reads as.

## Evidence

The full 855-test suite passes, but bats emits a warning:

```
The following warnings were encountered during tests:
BW02: Using flags on `run` requires at least BATS_VERSION=1.5.0. Use `bats_require_minimum_version 1.5.0` to fix this message.
      (from function `bats_warn_minimum_guaranteed_version' ...
       in test file tests/x-macos.bats, line 64)
```

Local bats is 1.14.0, so the flag works here and the test passes; the warning is the only signal.

## Impact

The suite is the repo's only test gate and runs both in `.pre-commit-config.yaml` (the `bats` local hook) and in `.github/workflows/tests.yml`, where bats comes from `mise-action` and its version is whatever `config/mise/config.toml` resolves. If that ever resolves below 1.5.0, this test stops checking the exit status it appears to check and instead tries to execute the flag as a command — and because the surrounding assertions still pass, it reports green while asserting nothing. A test that silently stops testing is worse than a missing one.

## Fix

Add the version declaration near the top of `tests/x-macos.bats`, before any `run` call:

```bash
bats_require_minimum_version 1.5.0
```

This turns the silent degradation into a hard error on an unsupported bats. Then re-run `bats tests/x-macos.bats` and confirm the BW02 warning is gone. Audit the other 78 `.bats` files the same way — grep for `run -` and `run !` and add the declaration wherever flags are used without it.

## Resolution
Added `bats_require_minimum_version 1.5.0` to tests/x-macos.bats above the setup() function, with a comment naming the failure mode (older bats treats the flag as the command and the assertion silently stops checking the exit status while still reporting ok). Verified: full suite exits 0 with 855 ok, 0 not ok, and the BW02 warning count is now 0 (was 1). Swept the other 78 .bats files for `run -N` / `run !` without the declaration — x-macos.bats was the only one, which matches bats having reported exactly one BW02.
title: `run` flags used without `bats_require_minimum_version`, so the assertion silently degrades on older bats

## Problem

`_acquire_lock` uses `ln(1)` as its atomic create-if-not-exists primitive, which is correct for the uncontended path. The stale-lock path is not atomic: it unlinks the pidfile with a bare `rm -f` and then re-creates it. Between one process's liveness check and its `rm -f`, another process can complete the whole reclaim and take the lock — and the first process then deletes the new owner's pidfile and links its own over the top.

## Evidence

`config/theme/_lib.sh:48-69`:

```bash
_acquire_lock()
{
  local pidfile=$1 tmp
  if [[ -e "$pidfile" ]]; then
    local pid
    pid=$(cat -- "$pidfile" 2> /dev/null || true)
    if [[ -n "$pid" ]] && kill -0 "$pid" 2> /dev/null; then
      return 1
    fi
    # Stale: remove and continue.
    rm -f -- "$pidfile"
  fi
  tmp="$(mktemp "${pidfile}.tmp.XXXXXX")"
  printf '%s\n' "$$" > "$tmp"
  if ln -- "$tmp" "$pidfile" 2> /dev/null; then
    rm -f -- "$tmp"
    return 0
  fi
  rm -f -- "$tmp"
  return 1
}
```

Losing interleaving, starting from a pidfile left by a SIGKILLed watcher (pid A, dead):

1. B reads pidfile -> A; `kill -0 A` fails -> stale.
2. C reads pidfile -> A; `kill -0 A` fails -> stale.
3. B runs `rm -f pidfile`, mktemps, `ln` succeeds. B holds the lock and proceeds past line 55 in `watcher`.
4. C, still executing its own stale branch, runs `rm -f -- "$pidfile"` — deleting B's live pidfile.
5. C mktemps, `ln` succeeds against the now-absent path. C also holds the lock.

Both daemons then run. The comment at line 45 claims "A loser in a race silently fails the ln and we return 1", which is true only while the pidfile stays present — it does not hold once step 4 can delete a live file.

The single caller is a singleton guard, `config/theme/watcher:55-60`:

```bash
if ! _acquire_lock "$pidfile"; then
  _log "INFO watcher: another instance holds $pidfile; exiting"
  exit 1
fi
trap 'rm -f "$pidfile"' EXIT INT TERM HUP
```

Concurrent starts are the normal case, not a corner case: the watcher is spawned from two independent shell-init paths — `config/exports:484` (bash and zsh) and `config/fish/config.fish:89` (fish). Opening a bash tab and a fish tab together, or a terminal restoring several panes at login, starts them in the same instant.

## Impact

Two watcher daemons poll the OS appearance and both call `apply` on every change. Each `apply` forks all five `handlers.d/` entries, so handlers run twice concurrently against the same targets — including `_idempotent_ln_sf` on shared symlinks and `_atomic_write` on the mode state file. Both also write the shared orchestrator log, which `_log` maintains under an explicitly documented "single-writer discipline", and both run its 200-line rotation (mktemp + mv), so one rotation can discard lines the other just wrote. Whichever daemon exits first fires `trap 'rm -f "$pidfile"'` and removes the pidfile out from under the survivor, leaving the lock unheld while a watcher is still running — so the next shell starts a third.

## Fix

Never unlink a lock you have not proven you own. Replace the unlink-then-link reclaim with an atomic `mv` replace plus an ownership read-back, which is portable to macOS (no `flock(1)` required) and makes a double-acquire impossible:

```bash
_acquire_lock()
{
  local pidfile=$1 tmp pid
  if [[ -e "$pidfile" ]]; then
    pid=$(cat -- "$pidfile" 2> /dev/null || true)
    if [[ -n "$pid" ]] && kill -0 "$pid" 2> /dev/null; then
      return 1
    fi
  fi
  tmp="$(mktemp "${pidfile}.tmp.XXXXXX")" || return 1
  printf '%s\n' "$$" > "$tmp"
  # Fast path: link wins only if no pidfile exists at all.
  if ln -- "$tmp" "$pidfile" 2> /dev/null; then
    rm -f -- "$tmp"
    return 0
  fi
  # Stale path: atomic replace, then confirm we are the winner. Racers all
  # mv; exactly one pid survives in the file, and only that process returns 0.
  mv -f -- "$tmp" "$pidfile" || { rm -f -- "$tmp"; return 1; }
  [[ "$(cat -- "$pidfile" 2> /dev/null)" == "$$" ]]
}
```

`mv -f` within one directory is `rename(2)`, which is atomic, so the file is never absent and the last writer is unambiguous. The read-back is what turns "we all wrote" into "one of us won".

Add a regression test to `tests/theme-watcher.bats` alongside the existing `watcher: second invocation exits 1 when first holds the lock` (line 113) — the current suite has exactly one lock test and no stale-pidfile case at all. Seed the pidfile with a definitely-dead pid, launch two acquires concurrently, and assert exactly one returns 0.

## Resolution
Rewrote _acquire_lock in config/theme/_lib.sh so ln(1) remains the only thing that grants the lock, and the stale-break's unlink-then-link pair now runs under a second ln-taken break lock ("${pidfile}.break"). A process that cannot take the break lock breaks nothing and returns 1.

Note the fix I first wrote was wrong and was caught before it landed: mv -f plus a read-back does NOT serialise anything, because each racer reads its own write (mv B, read B, mv C, read C) and every one concludes it won. Only serialising the break works.

Proven empirically rather than argued. Same 8-way race harness, 40 trials each, dead pid manufactured by spawning and reaping a subshell:
  OLD implementation: trials with MORE THAN ONE winner = 6 / 40
  NEW implementation: trials with MORE THAN ONE winner = 0 / 40

Two regression tests added to tests/theme-watcher.bats: "_acquire_lock: concurrent stale reclaim produces exactly one winner" (8 concurrent acquirers against a stale pidfile, asserts exactly 1) and "_acquire_lock: a live holder is never displaced" (asserts rc=1 and that the live pid is still the recorded owner). Both pass; the first is the one that fails against the old code.

Residual risk documented in the function comment rather than hidden: a process SIGKILLed while holding the break lock leaves the .break file and blocks future stale reclaim until removed by hand. That window is one cat + kill -0 + rm + ln, and it fails closed (no daemon) rather than open (two daemons).

Verification: bats tests/ rc=0, 857 ok, 0 not ok, 0 BW02 (up from 855 — the two new tests). shellcheck, bash -n, and shfmt --diff all clean on config/theme/_lib.sh. yarn lint rc=0.
title: Stale-lock reclaim in _acquire_lock is not atomic, so two watcher daemons can both hold the lock

## Problem

`config/shared.sh` defines an `array_diff` helper that nothing calls. It is parsed on every interactive bash and zsh startup, it uses `eval` on caller-supplied variable names, and it depends on `mapfile`, which zsh does not provide — so the one shell where half of these startups happen could never have run it successfully.

## Evidence

The definition, `config/shared.sh:155-176`:

```bash
if ! declare -f array_diff > /dev/null; then
  array_diff()
  {
    local result_var="$1"
    local arr1_name="$2"
    local arr2_name="$3"
    # shellcheck disable=SC1083,SC2086
    eval local ARR1=\(\"\${${arr1_name}[@]}\"\)
    # shellcheck disable=SC1083,SC2086
    eval local ARR2=\(\"\${${arr2_name}[@]}\"\)
    local IFS=$'\n'
    mapfile -t "$result_var" < <(comm -23 <(echo "${ARR1[*]}" | sort) <(echo "${ARR2[*]}" | sort))
    return 0
  }
fi
```

It is dead. Searching the whole repo outside its own definition returns nothing:

```
$ git grep -n 'array_diff' -- . ':!config/shared.sh' ':!docs/audit'
(empty)
```

No test references it either (`grep -rn 'array_diff' tests/` is empty).

`mapfile` is bash-only:

```
$ zsh -c 'whence mapfile || echo "mapfile NOT in zsh"'
mapfile NOT in zsh
```

And `config/shared.sh` is on the zsh startup path — `base/zshrc:14` does `source "$DOTFILES/config/shared.sh"` (bash reaches it via `base/bashrc:10`). `mapfile` also postdates bash 3.2, which is the floor `config/lib.sh:15` commits to ("Portable across bash 3.2+, bash 5, and zsh") and which macOS system bash still is.

The two `eval` lines are also the only `eval` in `config/shared.sh` that interpolates a caller-controlled string into shell syntax.

## Impact

No runtime failure today, precisely because nothing calls it — which is why a function that cannot work in zsh or on macOS system bash has survived. The cost is that it is a loaded gun in the shell-init hot path: the first caller added by someone reading the docstring gets a silent empty result in zsh (unset command, `mapfile` not found) or a hard failure on bash 3.2, in the one code path where a broken helper degrades every new terminal. It also contradicts the portability contract `config/lib.sh` states one file away, so a reader checking "does shared.sh respect the bash 3.2 floor?" gets the wrong answer.

## Fix

Delete lines 155-176 of `config/shared.sh`. Nothing imports it, no test covers it, and git history preserves it if a caller ever appears.

If a future caller genuinely needs set difference, write it without `eval` or `mapfile` by passing values rather than variable names:

```bash
# Prints lines present in $1 but not in $2, both newline-separated.
array_diff()
{
  comm -23 <(printf '%s\n' "$1" | sort) <(printf '%s\n' "$2" | sort)
}
```

That form works in bash 3.2, bash 5, and zsh alike, and the caller captures stdout instead of the function writing through a name.

Verify after deleting: `bash -n config/shared.sh`, `shellcheck config/shared.sh`, then `bats tests/` for the shell-entry-point coverage.

## Resolution
Deleted the dead array_diff block (22 lines) from config/shared.sh. Confirmed zero callers before removing (git grep outside its own definition returned nothing, no test referenced it), so nothing was rewired. Removing it takes the file's only eval-on-caller-supplied-name and its only bash-4-and-later builtin (mapfile, proven absent from zsh) out of the interactive shell-init path, restoring agreement with the bash 3.2+ floor stated at config/lib.sh:15.

Verification: `git grep -c array_diff -- config/` reports no references. shared.sh sources cleanly in both shells that load it — `bash source rc=0` and `zsh source rc=0` with DOTFILES set. shellcheck, bash -n, and shfmt --diff clean. bats tests/ rc=0 with 857 ok / 0 not ok, and yarn lint rc=0.

No replacement was added: nothing needed it. The finding records a non-eval, non-mapfile, value-passing form should a caller ever appear.
title: Dead `array_diff` helper is defined in every interactive shell and would break in zsh if ever called

## Problem

Line 106 carries `# nosec B603`, but B603 does not fire there. The only check that would report that line is B607 (`start_process_with_partial_path`), and `[tool.bandit] skips = ["B607"]` disables it globally. Bandit detects the mismatch and warns — twice, once per pass — on every invocation of the newly mandatory `yarn lint:bandit` step.

The suppression is not merely redundant: it is mislabelled. If B607 is ever removed from `skips` — the pyproject comment frames that skip as a deliberate, revisitable decision — line 106 will start failing the gate despite carrying what looks like an approved suppression.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">`local/bin/x-git-largest-files.py:106`:

```python
git_dir = check_output(["git", "rev-parse", "--git-dir"]).decode("utf-8").strip()  # nosec B603 # nosemgrep
```

Bandit's own report, run exactly as the gate runs it:

```
$ bandit -c pyproject.toml local/bin/x-git-largest-files.py
[main]    INFO     profile exclude tests: B607
[tester]  WARNING  nosec encountered (B603), but no failed test on file ./local/bin/x-git-largest-files.py:106
[tester]  WARNING  nosec encountered (B603), but no failed test on file ./local/bin/x-git-largest-files.py:106
          No issues identified.
```

The same two lines appear in the `yarn lint` output, and are the only non-"No issues found" text the whole gate emits.

`pyproject.toml`, `[tool.bandit]`:

```toml
skips = ["B607"]
```

Line 111 is the contrast case — there `# nosec B603` is doing real work and draws no warning:

```python
verify_pack = Popen(  # nosec B603
```</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">`yarn lint` is the Stop-hook gate, so these two WARNING lines are printed on every turn that touches the gate. A gate whose clean state includes a standing warning trains the reader to skim past bandit's output, which is where a real new suppression mismatch would also appear. Second-order: the annotation records a decision about B603 at a line where no B603 decision was ever made, so the next reader inherits a wrong premise.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Drop the inaccurate code from the annotation and keep the semgrep suppression, which is real:

```python
git_dir = check_output(["git", "rev-parse", "--git-dir"]).decode("utf-8").strip()  # nosemgrep
```

Verify the warning is gone and nothing new fires:

```
bandit -c pyproject.toml local/bin/x-git-largest-files.py
```

Expect `No issues identified.` with no WARNING lines. If B607 is ever taken out of `skips`, this line needs `# nosec B607` — with the reasoning already recorded in the `[tool.bandit]` comment — not `B603`.</fix>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
Wrong: the `# nosec B603` on line 106 is load-bearing, and bandit's warning is a false diagnostic. Removing the suppression makes B603 fire on that exact line and takes the gate from High: 0 to High: 1 — `bandit -c pyproject.toml` on a copy with the annotation stripped reports `>> Issue: [B603:subprocess_without_shell_equals_true] ... High: 1`. The finding read "nosec encountered (B603), but no failed test" as proof the check never fires there; it is the opposite. Bandit evaluates "did a test fail at this line?" after applying the suppression, so a *successfully* suppressed B603 always reports as "no failed test". Reordering to `# nosemgrep # nosec B603` was also tested and does not silence it, so the trailing semgrep annotation is not the cause either. Two WARNING lines on every `yarn lint` are the cost of a correct suppression, not a defect in this repo. Attempted fix was applied, measured, and fully reverted (`git checkout -- local/bin/x-git-largest-files.py`); the file is unchanged from HEAD.
title: Dead `# nosec B603` on line 106 makes bandit print a warning on every yarn lint run

## Problem

The working tree adds `lint:bandit` to the aggregate `lint` script in `package.json` and pins `"pipx:bandit[toml]" = "1.9.4"` in `config/mise/config.toml`. That file is the *global* mise config, symlinked to `~/.config/mise/`. CI never sees it. The `lint` job in `.github/workflows/tests.yml` installs tools with `jdx/mise-action`, which reads the repo's `.mise.toml` — and bandit was not added there.

`.mise.toml` states this contract in its own comment (lines 6-9): "These are also pinned in config/mise/config.toml (the global config, symlinked to ~/.config/mise/), which is what provides them on a workstation. CI checks out the repo and never sees that file, so the gate needs them here too." The bandit change honoured only half of it.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">`package.json` (working tree) — bandit is now a mandatory link in the chain:

```
"lint:bandit": "bandit -c pyproject.toml -r . -q",
"lint": "yarn lint:biome && ... && yarn lint:usage && yarn lint:bandit",
```

`.mise.toml` in full — no bandit, and no `python.default_packages_file` that could supply one:

```
[tools]
node = "26.5.1"
python = "3.14"
go = "1.26.5"
biome = "2.5.2"
editorconfig-checker = "3.8.0"
usage = "3.6.0"
"npm:prettier" = "3.9.6"
"npm:markdownlint-cli" = "0.49.1"
"npm:markdown-table-formatter" = "1.7.0"
"npm:v8r" = "6.1.0"
```

`mise ls --current` run from the repo root confirms the source and that the pinned entry is not even installed locally:

```
biome         2.5.2            ~/.dotfiles/.mise.toml      2.5.2
pipx:bandit   1.9.4 (missing)  ~/.config/mise/config.toml  1.9.4
python        3.14.6           ~/.dotfiles/.mise.toml      3.14
```

`.github/workflows/tests.yml:69-76` — the job that breaks:

```yaml
- name: Install the mise toolchain
  uses: jdx/mise-action@7e36c90d9ab29c415a2384db3006f3ec8a8cc654 # v4.2.4
- name: Enable corepack for the pinned yarn
  run: corepack enable
- name: Run lint
  run: yarn lint
```

`ubuntu-latest` ships no `bandit`, so `yarn lint:bandit` exits 127 and the job fails. The change is still uncommitted, so no CI run has surfaced this yet.

Secondary: the `bandit` currently satisfying `yarn lint` on the workstation resolves to `~/.local/share/mise/installs/python/3.14/bin/bandit` (from `config/mise/default-python-packages`), not the newly pinned `pipx:bandit[toml]`, which mise reports as `(missing)`. The `[toml]` extra the new comment calls "required" is therefore not what is being exercised today.</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">The first push or PR carrying this change red-lights the `Lint (yarn lint)` job on `tests.yml`. Because `linters.yml` only runs on `pull_request`, a direct push to `main` hits the same failure with no second gate to disambiguate it. Locally `yarn lint` passes, so the failure appears only in CI and reads as a runner problem rather than a missing pin.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Add the same pin to `.mise.toml`, next to the other `yarn lint` tools, keeping the two copies renovate already tracks in step:

```toml
"npm:v8r" = "6.1.0"
"pipx:bandit[toml]" = "1.9.4"
```

Then verify the CI path rather than the workstation path — `mise ls --current` must show `.mise.toml` as bandit's source, and the entry must not read `(missing)`:

```
mise install
mise ls --current | grep bandit
yarn lint:bandit
```

If `pipx:bandit` stays `(missing)` after `mise install`, the pipx backend is not resolving and `yarn lint` is passing on the `default-python-packages` copy by accident; fix that before relying on the pin.</fix>
</invoke>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
Added `"pipx:bandit[toml]" = "1.9.4"` to `.mise.toml` beside the other `yarn lint` tools, with a comment stating why the [toml] extra is required. Verified per the finding's own acceptance step: `mise install "pipx:bandit[toml]@1.9.4"` succeeded ("Installed 3 executables: bandit, bandit-baseline, bandit-config-generator"), and `mise ls --current` now reports `pipx:bandit 1.9.4 ~/.dotfiles/.mise.toml` — source is the repo manifest CI reads, and no longer `(missing)`. `yarn lint` rc=0.

## Problem

`__pushover_send_message` assembles the whole curl invocation into the string `curl_cmd`, interpolating `${message}`, `${title}`, `${url}`, `${device}` and every other flag value, then runs `eval "${curl_cmd}"`. `eval` re-parses that string as shell source, so any command substitution or quote character in a value is executed rather than transmitted.

Both classic vectors work: `$(...)` inside a value is expanded by `eval`, and a `"` in a value closes the quoting and lets the rest of the argument be parsed as commands. Quoting at the call site does not help — the caller's quotes are consumed before the value ever reaches `curl_cmd`.

`.claude/hooks/notify-idle.sh` is an in-repo caller that routes hook-supplied text straight into it. That file already recognises the threat model in its other branch: line 10 reads "Pass $msg as argv so AppleScript never parses it as code." The `osascript` path is hardened; the `pushover` path — which is tried first — is not.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">`local/bin/pushover:58-75`:

```sh
curl_cmd="\"${CURL}\" -s -S \
  ${CURL_OPTS} \
  -F \"token=${TOKEN}\" \
  -F \"user=${USER}\" \
  -F \"message=${message}\" \
  $(__pushover_opt_field title "${title}") \
  ...
  \"${PUSHOVER_URL}\""

response="$(eval "${curl_cmd}")"
```

Run against a stub `curl` that echoes its argv, with the payload single-quoted so the calling shell expands nothing:

```
$ PATH="$stub:$PATH" PUSHOVER_TOKEN=tok PUSHOVER_USER=usr \
    sh local/bin/pushover 'hello $(id -u) end'
ARGS: -s -S -F token=tok -F user=usr -F message=hello 1000 end https://api.pushover.net/1/messages.json
```

`$(id -u)` ran; `1000` is this account's uid, not the literal text.

Quote-breaking gives full statement injection:

```
$ PATH="$stub:$PATH" PUSHOVER_TOKEN=tok PUSHOVER_USER=usr \
    sh local/bin/pushover 'a"; echo INJECTED_MARKER >&2; echo "b'
ARGS: -s -S -F token=tok -F user=usr -F message=a
INJECTED_MARKER
{"status":1}
```

The injected `echo` executed as a separate command.

`.claude/hooks/notify-idle.sh:5-15` — the untrusted path in:

```sh
msg=$(jq -r '.message // "Claude is waiting for input"')

if command -v pushover > /dev/null; then
  pushover "Claude Code" "$msg"
elif command -v osascript > /dev/null; then
  # Pass $msg as argv so AppleScript never parses it as code.
  osascript ... -- "$msg"
fi
```</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">Arbitrary command execution with the invoking user's privileges whenever a message contains `$(`, backticks, or a double quote. Notification bodies are exactly the wrong place to assume clean input — the common use is `pushover "backup failed: $(tail -1 log)"`, `pushover "branch $BRANCH deployed"`, or, as here, a hook forwarding text produced elsewhere. `notify-idle.sh` fires on every idle notification and prefers the vulnerable branch, so on any machine with `pushover` on PATH the hardened `osascript` path is never reached.

Secondary exposure in the same statement: `-F "token=${TOKEN}"` is inside the eval'd string, so the API token is subject to the same re-parsing and appears in any shell trace of the eval.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Delete the string-building and `eval`. POSIX `sh` has no arrays but `set --` accumulates argv exactly as needed, and `__pushover_opt_field` collapses into an append:

```sh
# Append `-F field=value` to the argument list when value is non-empty.
# Values go in as single argv entries, so no shell parsing ever sees them.
__pushover_opt_field()
{
  [ -n "$2" ] || return 0
  set -- "$1" "$2"
  ARGS_FIELD="$1" ARGS_VALUE="$2"
}

__pushover_send_message()
{
  device="${1:-}"

  set -- -s -S \
    -F "token=${TOKEN}" \
    -F "user=${USER}" \
    -F "message=${message}"

  [ -n "$device" ]    && set -- "$@" -F "device=$device"
  [ -n "$callback" ]  && set -- "$@" -F "callback=$callback"
  [ -n "$timestamp" ] && set -- "$@" -F "timestamp=$timestamp"
  [ -n "$priority" ]  && set -- "$@" -F "priority=$priority"
  [ -n "$retry" ]     && set -- "$@" -F "retry=$retry"
  [ -n "$expire" ]    && set -- "$@" -F "expire=$expire"
  [ -n "$title" ]     && set -- "$@" -F "title=$title"
  [ -n "$sound" ]     && set -- "$@" -F "sound=$sound"
  [ -n "$url" ]       && set -- "$@" -F "url=$url"
  [ -n "$url_title" ] && set -- "$@" -F "url_title=$url_title"

  response="$("$CURL" "$@" "$PUSHOVER_URL")"
  ...
}
```

Drop `__pushover_opt_field` and `CURL_OPTS` entirely — the former exists only to emit shell text for the eval, and the latter is initialised to `""` at line 99 and never assigned anywhere.

Add a regression test to `tests/pushover.bats` asserting the payload is transmitted literally, using the same stub-curl seam as above:

```bash
@test "pushover: command substitution in a message is not executed" {
  run pushover 'hello $(id -u) end'
  [ "$status" -eq 0 ]
  grep -q 'message=hello \$(id -u) end' "$STUB/args"
}
```

While in the file, two adjacent defects worth the same commit: line 98 assigns `USER=$PUSHOVER_USER`, clobbering the standard `USER` variable for the rest of the process — rename it `PUSHOVER_USER_KEY`; and neither `TOKEN` nor `USER` is checked for emptiness before the request, so a missing credential produces an opaque API error instead of a usage message.</fix>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
Removed the `eval` entirely. `__pushover_send_message` now accumulates argv with `set --` and calls `"${CURL}" "$@" "${PUSHOVER_URL}"`; `__pushover_opt_field` and the never-assigned `CURL_OPTS` are gone. Both PoCs now transmit literally instead of executing: `pushover 'hello $(id -u) end'` sends `message=hello $(id -u) end` (was `message=hello 1000 end`), and the quote-break payload no longer runs its injected `echo`. Also renamed the `USER` clobber to `PUSHOVER_USER_KEY` and added empty-credential guards that fail before any request. Covered by 7 new assertions in tests/pushover.bats (10 total, all pass), including a multi-word-title case proving values stay single argv entries. `sh -n` and shellcheck clean.
title: pushover builds its curl command as a string and evals it, so any message content executes as shell code

## Problem

`config/exports:12` and `config/fish/exports.fish:7` export `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR="$HOME/.local/run"` whenever the session has not set one — always the case on macOS, and on any Linux login that bypasses pam_systemd. `dotbot-links.yaml` creates that directory with no `mode:`, so it inherits the repo-wide default of `0755` from `tools/dotbot-defaults.yaml`.

The XDG Base Directory Specification is not permissive about this directory: "The directory MUST be owned by the user, and he MUST be the only one having read and write access to it. Its Unix access mode MUST be 0700." Every program that honours `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` puts sockets, lock files and short-lived credential material there on the assumption that mode holds.

The repo already knows the mechanism — `~/.ssh`, `~/.ssh/local.d` and `~/.local/share/gnupg` each carry an explicit `mode: 0700` in the same `create:` block. The runtime dir was left out.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">`dotbot-links.yaml` `create:` block, annotated by whether the next line supplies a mode:

```
none ~/.local/run:
none ~/.local/state:
none ~/.local/state/tmux:
none ~/.local/state/zsh:
MODE ~/.local/share/gnupg:      <- mode: 0700
MODE ~/.ssh:                    <- mode: 0700
MODE ~/.ssh/local.d:            <- mode: 0700
```

`tools/dotbot-defaults.yaml` supplies the fallback:

```yaml
- defaults:
    create:
      mode: 0755
```

`config/exports:12`:

```sh
[ -z "${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-}" ] && export XDG_RUNTIME_DIR="$HOME/.local/run"
```

On the maintainer's machine the directory is worse than the declared default — `stat -c '%a %n'` reports:

```
777 /home/ivuorinen/.local/run
700 /home/ivuorinen/.ssh
777 /home/ivuorinen/.local/state
```

0755 is the best case this config can produce; 0777 is what it actually left behind (see the companion finding on creation-only modes).</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">On any host with more than one local account — a work machine with a service user, a shared box, a container that runs as a second uid — every other local user can list and read whatever lands in `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`. At the observed 0777 they can also write it: replace a socket with their own, or plant a file where a program expects to create one. The exposure is silent, because nothing in the repo checks the mode after installation.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Give the runtime dir the same treatment as `~/.ssh` in `dotbot-links.yaml`:

```yaml
    ~/.local/run:
      mode: 0700
```

`~/.local/state` deserves the same, since `config/exports` puts zsh history (`$XDG_STATE_HOME/zsh/history`), the 1Password cache (`$XDG_STATE_HOME/1password`) and the theme daemon's pidfile under it:

```yaml
    ~/.local/state:
      mode: 0700
```

This alone will not repair the machines already at 0777 — dotbot skips paths that exist. Apply the companion finding's fix as well, or chmod once by hand:

```
chmod 0700 ~/.local/run ~/.local/state
```</fix>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
Added `mode: 0700` to `~/.local/run` (XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, per the XDG spec's mandatory 0700) and to `~/.local/state`, `~/.local/state/tmux`, `~/.local/state/zsh` in dotbot-links.yaml, each with a comment naming what it protects. Declared modes now read: 0700 for run/state/state-tmux/state-zsh/gnupg/ssh/ssh-local.d, default 0755 for the cache and share paths. yamllint and prettier both clean. Note the drift on already-provisioned machines is a separate matter, handled by audit-066b5404's `dfm check perms`.
title: XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (~/.local/run) is created world-readable, against the XDG spec's mandatory 0700

## Problem

`./install` is documented and used as a re-runnable operation — `./install --links` exists precisely to refresh state. For directory permissions it is not: dotbot's `create` plugin applies the declared `mode:` only when the path does not yet exist. On every subsequent run it logs "Path exists" and returns success without looking at the mode.

That makes every `mode:` in `dotbot-links.yaml` a one-shot assertion tied to the moment a machine was first provisioned. Adding or tightening a mode later — including the `mode: 0700` fix for `~/.local/run` — is a no-op on every machine that already has the directory, while `./install` still exits 0. `dfm check` does not cover the gap either: it contains no `stat`, `chmod`, or permission logic at all.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">`tools/dotbot/src/dotbot/plugins/create.py:47-61`:

```python
def _create(self, path: str, mode: int) -> bool:
    success = True
    if not self._exists(path):
        self._log.debug(f"Trying to create path {path} with mode {mode}")
        try:
            self._log.lowinfo(f"Creating path {path}")
            os.makedirs(path, mode)
            os.chmod(path, mode)
        except OSError:
            self._log.warning(f"Failed to create path {path}")
            success = False
    else:
        self._log.lowinfo(f"Path exists {path}")
    return success
```

The `else` branch is the whole defect: an existing path is never chmod'ed.

Observed drift on the maintainer's machine, against a config whose default is `mode: 0755`:

```
$ stat -c '%a %n' ~/.local/run ~/.local/state ~/.local/state/zsh ~/.local/state/tmux
777 /home/ivuorinen/.local/run
777 /home/ivuorinen/.local/state
777 /home/ivuorinen/.local/state/zsh
777 /home/ivuorinen/.local/state/tmux
```

`./install` has been run many times against this tree and has corrected none of them.

`dfm check` has no permission coverage:

```
$ grep -nE 'stat |chmod|perm|mode|0700|0755' local/bin/dfm-check
(no output)
```</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">Every permission hardening added to `dotbot-links.yaml` after a machine's first provisioning is silently inert on that machine, and `./install` reports success. The `mode: 0700` entries on `~/.ssh`, `~/.ssh/local.d` and `~/.local/share/gnupg` are only as good as the day each host was set up. A drift introduced by any other tool — the 0777 above — persists indefinitely with no gate that notices.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Add a permission check to `dfm check`, which is already the repo's "is this machine correctly set up" command, and have it read the declared modes rather than a second hardcoded list:

```bash
# dfm-check: verify declared create modes still hold.
python3 - <<'PY' | while read -r want path; do
  have=$(stat -c '%a' "$path" 2>/dev/null) || continue
  [ "$have" = "$want" ] || msgr warn "mode drift: $path is $have, expected $want"
done
import os, re, yaml
doc = yaml.safe_load(open("dotbot-links.yaml"))
default = 755
for block in doc:
    for path, opts in (block.get("create") or {}).items():
        mode = (opts or {}).get("mode", default)
        print(f"{mode:o} {os.path.expanduser(path)}")
PY
```

Then add `mode: 0700` to `~/.local/run` and `~/.local/state` per the companion finding, and chmod the existing directories once by hand — the check will keep them honest from then on.

Do not "fix" this by patching `tools/dotbot/`: it is a submodule and `.claude/rules/vendored-files.md` forbids editing it. A repair belongs in `dfm check`, not upstream.</fix>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
Added a `perms` subcommand to `dfm check`, wired into `dfm check all`, the MENU, and the `#USAGE` tree. It parses the declared modes straight out of dotbot-links.yaml with awk (falling back to the `create.mode` default in tools/dotbot-defaults.yaml), so there is no second hardcoded list to drift; comment lines inside the create block are skipped, and absent paths are ignored since several entries are host-specific. Uses `stat -c '%a'` with a `stat -f '%Lp'` fallback for BSD/macOS. Verified both directions: against this machine it reports the real drift and exits 1 (`mode drift: /home/ivuorinen/.local/run is 0777, declared 0700` + a paste-ready `chmod 0700 ...` line), and against a synthetic fixture whose modes match it reports "All 2 created directories match their declared mode" and exits 0. shellcheck -x and shfmt clean. Deliberately did not touch tools/dotbot — it is a submodule under .claude/rules/vendored-files.md.
title: Declared create modes are applied only at first creation, so ./install never repairs a drifted permission and nothing detects one

## Problem

`.claude/rules/bash-routing.md` names exactly one git reader that stays on `Bash`: "`git status` is the one git reader the hook lets through, with or without `-s`: it is a common one-line check." `pre-bash-route.sh` repeats the promise in its own comment at lines 59-60.

The implementation does not keep it. `status` is absent from `allow_git_subcmd_re`, and the git branch denies any subcommand not on that list. So `git status` is denied on every invocation, with a reason that says the subcommand "is not on the allow list (output-reader)" — contradicting the rule the reason cites.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">`pre-bash-route.sh:51` — the allow list, with `status` missing:

```
allow_git_subcmd_re='^(add|commit|mv|rm|checkout|push|fetch|reset|restore|stash|tag|init|clone|branch|merge|remote|cherry-pick|revert|switch|am|apply|format-patch|gc|prune|reflog|worktree|notes|submodule|rerere|update-ref|symbolic-ref|update-index|hash-object|cat-file|rev-parse|rev-list|ls-files|check-ignore|config)$'
```

`pre-bash-route.sh:59-60` — the comment it contradicts:

```
# Note: `git status` (with or without `-s`) is _allowed_ — it's a common one-line
# check. `git log/diff/show/blame` always produce reviewable output and route through
```

Feeding the hook its own PreToolUse JSON:

```
$ printf '{"tool_input":{"command":"git status"}}' | bash .claude/hooks/pre-bash-route.sh \
    | jq -r .hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision
deny
```

For contrast, the cases that are meant to deny do deny, so the guard is otherwise working:

```
git log --oneline -5   -> deny
yarn lint              -> deny
cat README.md          -> deny
```</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">`git status` is the most frequent one-line check in this repo's workflow, and it is blocked on every attempt. Each block costs a round trip and pushes a one-line query into `ctx_batch_execute`, which the rule explicitly says is not required for it. Worse for the enforcement chain as a whole: the denial reason cites `bash-routing.md`, so an agent that reads the rule to resolve the conflict finds the rule saying the opposite of what just happened. A guard that contradicts its own documentation trains the reader to distrust both, which is the failure mode `no-hook-bypass.md` depends on not happening.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Add `status` to the git allow list in `pre-bash-route.sh:51`:

```
allow_git_subcmd_re='^(status|add|commit|mv|rm|checkout|push|fetch|reset|restore|stash|tag|init|clone|branch|merge|remote|cherry-pick|revert|switch|am|apply|format-patch|gc|prune|reflog|worktree|notes|submodule|rerere|update-ref|symbolic-ref|update-index|hash-object|cat-file|rev-parse|rev-list|ls-files|check-ignore|config)$'
```

Verify both directions, since the deny cases must not regress:

```bash
for c in "git status" "git status -s" "git log --oneline" "git diff"; do
  printf '{"tool_input":{"command":"%s"}}' "$c" \
    | bash .claude/hooks/pre-bash-route.sh \
    | jq -r --arg c "$c" '$c + " -> " + (.hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision // "allow")'
done
```

Expect allow, allow, deny, deny.

The hook has no test file. Add `tests/pre-bash-route.bats` covering that table — every claim `bash-routing.md` makes about a specific command is a test case, and this defect is precisely what such a test would have caught.</fix>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
Added `status` to `allow_git_subcmd_re` in .claude/hooks/pre-bash-route.sh, with a comment recording why it is there so it is not dropped again. Verified in both directions via the new tests/pre-bash-route.bats: `git status` and `git status -s` now return allow, while `git log`, `git diff`, `git show` and `git blame` still deny. The hook now matches what .claude/rules/bash-routing.md and its own lines 59-60 say.
title: `git status` is denied by the router although the rule and the hook's own comment both promise it is allowed

## Problem

The router decides using `first_word()` on each pipeline segment, after `strip_env_prefix()` removes `env VAR=…` and inline `VAR=…` prefixes. That covers exactly two wrapper shapes. Everything else that puts a different token in first position walks straight through:

- an absolute or relative path (`/bin/cat`) — the deny regex is anchored `^cat$`;
- a shell wrapper (`command`, `nohup`, `time`, `timeout`, `stdbuf`, `xargs`) — the wrapper is the first word, the denied command is the second;
- `env -i` — `strip_env_prefix` strips `env ` but its `VAR=` group matches zero times, leaving `-i` as the first word;
- a backslash-escaped name (`\cat`) — quoting-removal is a shell step the hook never performs.

`/bin/bash -c '<denied>'` is the sharpest case: lines 54-55 add `bash|sh|zsh|dash|ksh` to the deny list specifically "to block `bash -c '<denied>'` … bypasses called out in no-hook-bypass.md", and prefixing the interpreter with its own path defeats that in one character class.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">Each command below was fed to the hook as PreToolUse JSON; `deny` means blocked, blank means no decision (the call proceeds):

```
cat README.md                              -> deny
/bin/cat README.md                         ->
command cat README.md                      ->
timeout 5 rg foo .                         ->
nohup grep foo README.md                   ->
git ls-files | xargs cat                   ->
env -i cat README.md                       ->
\cat README.md                             ->
/bin/bash -c "cat README.md"               ->
```

The relevant code, `pre-bash-route.sh:100-121`:

```sh
first_word()
{
  local segment=$1
  printf '%s' "$segment" | awk '{print $1}'
  return 0
}

strip_env_prefix()
{
  local segment=$1
  printf '%s' "$segment" | sed -E '
    s/^env[[:space:]]+([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z_0-9]*=[^[:space:]]+[[:space:]]+)*//
    s/^([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z_0-9]*=[^[:space:]]+[[:space:]]+)+//
  '
  return 0
}
```

`pre-bash-route.sh:53-56` states the intent the evidence defeats:

```sh
# Denylist: first-word commands that almost always produce reviewable output.
# Includes `bash`/`sh`/`zsh`/`dash`/`ksh` to block `bash -c '<denied>'` and
# `bash <<EOF<denied>EOF` heredoc bypasses called out in no-hook-bypass.md.
```</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">The router is the mechanical half of the context-window protection; `bash-routing.md` and `no-hook-bypass.md` are the prose half. `no-hook-bypass.md` already forbids these forms by policy — "using `Bash -c '…'` / heredoc tricks to hide a denied command inside an allowed one all count as bypass" — so an agent taking any of them is out of compliance. The defect is that nothing stops it: a single unrouted `/bin/cat` on a large file dumps the file into context, which is the exact failure the whole chain exists to prevent, and it does so while reporting no violation. The `BASH_OK` marker exists as the documented, visible escape hatch; these seven are undocumented and invisible ones.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Normalise the token before matching, in two steps.

Basename-and-unescape the first word so a path or backslash cannot hide a name:

```sh
# Reduce a command token to its bare name: strip any leading directory
# component and a backslash escape, so `/bin/cat` and `\cat` both match the
# `cat` entry on the deny list.
normalise_cmd()
{
  local w=${1#\\}
  printf '%s' "${w##*/}"
}
```

Peel transparent wrappers until a real command name is in first position, mirroring what `strip_env_prefix` already does for `env`:

```sh
# Wrappers that execute their argument list: the denied command is the next
# word, not the first. Loop, because `nohup timeout 5 rg …` nests them.
strip_wrappers()
{
  local seg=$1
  while :; do
    case "$(normalise_cmd "$(first_word "$seg")")" in
      command | builtin | exec | nohup | time | timeout | stdbuf | xargs | nice | ionice)
        seg=$(printf '%s' "$seg" | sed -E 's/^[^[:space:]]+[[:space:]]+//')
        # Drop the wrapper's own flags and its numeric argument (timeout 5).
        seg=$(printf '%s' "$seg" | sed -E 's/^(-[^[:space:]]+[[:space:]]+|[0-9]+[a-z]?[[:space:]]+)*//')
        ;;
      *) break ;;
    esac
  done
  printf '%s' "$seg"
}
```

Call both in the loop at line 127:

```sh
segment=$(strip_env_prefix "$segment")
segment=$(strip_wrappers "$segment")
fw=$(normalise_cmd "$(first_word "$segment")")
```

`env -i` falls out of this too, once `strip_env_prefix` also drops leading flags:

```sh
    s/^env[[:space:]]+(-[^[:space:]]+[[:space:]]+)*([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z_0-9]*=[^[:space:]]+[[:space:]]+)*//
```

Then lock the behaviour down in `tests/pre-bash-route.bats` with the nine-row table above as the fixture — the hook currently has no test file at all, which is why a deny list can drift from its own comment without anything noticing.</fix>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
Added `normalise_cmd` (strips a leading backslash and any directory component, so `/bin/cat` and `\cat` match the anchored deny entries) and `strip_wrappers` (peels command/builtin/exec/nohup/time/timeout/stdbuf/xargs/nice/ionice plus their flags and numeric args, looping for nested wrappers), and extended `strip_env_prefix` to drop `env`'s own flags so `env -i` no longer leaves `-i` in first position. The main loop now calls both before matching. All seven bypasses from the finding now deny: `/bin/cat`, `command cat`, `timeout 5 rg`, `nohup grep`, `git ls-files | xargs cat`, `env -i cat`, `\cat`, plus `/bin/bash -c "cat …"` and `/usr/bin/grep`. `command -v X` is explicitly exempted from wrapper stripping — it is a probe that never executes X — and is asserted to stay allowed. Locked down by 15 tests in the new tests/pre-bash-route.bats, all passing; full suite 879/879 green.
title: Seven trivial command forms bypass the bash router: absolute paths, wrapper commands, and xargs
