## Problem

`LICENSE` and `package.json` both declare the whole repository MIT. The tree includes `local/bin/iterm2_shell_integration.zsh`, which carries a GNU GPL v2-or-later header, plus five vendored fish plugin functions and six vendored fzf files whose upstream licenses are recorded nowhere in the distribution. There is no `NOTICE` or `THIRD-PARTY` file.

The GPL header itself is intact in the file, which is the part that matters most — the notice travels with the code. What is wrong is the repo-level claim: a reader (or an automated license scanner, or anyone copying from this repo) is told "MIT" for a tree that is not uniformly MIT. `.claude/rules/vendored-files.md` names every upstream and its URL, but that file is an agent rule, not a license declaration, and it records no license for any entry.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">`LICENSE:1-3` and `package.json:35`:

```
MIT License

Copyright (c) 2022 Ismo Vuorinen
```

```json
"license": "MIT",
```

`local/bin/iterm2_shell_integration.zsh:2-14`:

```
# This program is free software; you can redistribute it and/or
# modify it under the terms of the GNU General Public License
# as published by the Free Software Foundation; either version 2
# of the License, or (at your option) any later version.
...
# You should have received a copy of the GNU General Public License
# along with this program; if not, write to the Free Software
# Foundation, Inc., 51 Franklin Street, Fifth Floor, Boston, MA  02110-1301, USA.
```

No attribution file exists:

```
$ ls NOTICE THIRD-PARTY*
ls: cannot access 'NOTICE': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access 'THIRD-PARTY*': No such file or directory
```

The other vendored files carry no license header at all in their first eight lines — `local/bin/fzf-tmux`, `config/fzf/key-bindings.bash`, `config/fish/functions/fisher.fish`, `config/fish/functions/bass.fish`, `config/fish/functions/__z_add.fish`. `.claude/skills/graphify/` contains only `SKILL.md` and `references/`, no license file.

`.claude/rules/vendored-files.md` lists every upstream URL and, for the fish group, a table of projects — but no license column and no license text.</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">A public repository that says MIT while distributing GPL-2.0-or-later code misrepresents its own terms. Anyone who takes the repo at its word and copies `iterm2_shell_integration.zsh` into a proprietary or MIT project inherits a GPL obligation they were told did not exist. License scanners run against the repo (Codacy, Snyk, and the `license` lens of this audit) will flag the conflict on every run with nothing in-tree to reconcile it against. The fzf and fish files have the opposite problem — their licenses are permissive, but nothing in the distribution says so, so a downstream reader cannot establish they are safe to reuse.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Add a `NOTICE` file at the repo root enumerating each vendored tree, its upstream and its license, and point `LICENSE` at it. Draw the entries straight from the table `.claude/rules/vendored-files.md` already maintains:

```markdown
# Third-party components

The MIT license in LICENSE covers this repository's own work. The files
below are vendored from upstream projects and keep their own terms.

| Path                                    | Upstream                          | License           |
|-----------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|-------------------|
| `local/bin/iterm2_shell_integration.zsh`| iTerm2                            | GPL-2.0-or-later  |
| `local/bin/fzf-tmux`, `config/fzf/*`    | junegunn/fzf                      | MIT               |
| `config/fish/functions/fisher.fish`     | jorgebucaran/fisher               | MIT               |
| `config/fish/functions/bass.fish`, `__bass.py` | edc/bass                   | MIT               |
| `config/fish/functions/__z_add.fish`, `__z_clean.fish` | jethrokuan/z      | MIT               |
| `.claude/skills/graphify/`              | (record upstream + license)       |                   |
```

Add one line to `LICENSE` above the MIT text: `Portions of this repository are third-party; see NOTICE.` Confirm each license against the upstream repo before writing it down rather than assuming MIT — the `no-schema-guessing` discipline applies to license facts too.

Add the `NOTICE` row to `.claude/rules/vendored-files.md`'s maintenance instructions so the two stay in step, the same way `.codacy.yml`, `pyproject.toml` and `.mega-linter.yml` are already kept in step there.</fix>

## Evidence

## Impact

## Fix

## Resolution
Added a root `NOTICE` enumerating every vendored tree with its upstream and license, and prefixed `LICENSE` with a pointer to it stating the repo is not uniformly MIT. Licenses were established from the GitHub license API in this session rather than assumed: junegunn/fzf MIT, jorgebucaran/fisher MIT, edc/bass MIT, jethrokuan/z MIT (all HTTP 200). iTerm2 shell integration is recorded as GPL-2.0-or-later from the notice preserved in the file's own header. The graphify skill is recorded as "license not recorded" with an instruction to verify against the plugin source before redistributing — deliberately not guessed, per .claude/rules/no-schema-guessing.md. NOTICE carries a Maintenance section naming itself as the fourth copy of the vendored list, alongside the rule frontmatter, .codacy.yml exclude_paths, and [tool.bandit] exclude_dirs. `yarn lint` rc=0.
title: Repo declares MIT while shipping a GPL-2.0-or-later file, and carries no attribution for any vendored upstream

## Problem

The `local/bin` loop picks a file as a usage spec when `#USAGE` or `//USAGE` appears anywhere in it, at any column. `local/bin/CLAUDE.md` documents the convention and writes the directive inline in prose, so the markdown file was handed to `usage` as if it were a script. `usage` rejected it as invalid KDL once per output format — fish, bash and zsh completions plus markdown and manpage — and the accumulated `errors` count became the script's exit status.

`usage` only extracts directives that start the line, and `scripts/install-completions.sh` already knows this: the dfm assembly step greps `'^#USAGE'` at lines 148 and 152, and the comment at lines 137-140 spells out that "usage only extracts #USAGE directives when the file looks like a script". The selector at line 116 was the one place that did not anchor.

The trap is structural rather than specific to one file: any note, README, or doc under `local/bin/` that mentions the directive in prose selects itself as a spec.</problem>
<parameter name="evidence">`scripts/install-completions.sh:114-116` before the fix:

```sh
for spec in "$DOTFILES"/local/bin/*; do
  [[ -f "$spec" ]] || continue
  grep -q '#USAGE\|//USAGE' "$spec" 2> /dev/null || continue
```

The prose that matched, `local/bin/CLAUDE.md:18` and `:42`:

```markdown
  — one file per section, each carrying its own `#USAGE` subtree.
per-section `#USAGE` fragments into one `dfm` spec (skipping `dfm`/`dfm-*`
```

Running the generator:

```

rc=4
```

`CLAUDE.md` was the only failure; all five warnings name it.

Anchoring costs nothing, because every real spec already complies:

```
match anywhere: 88   match at column 0: 87
would be DROPPED by anchoring: CLAUDE.md
```

Every `scripts/*.sh` also carries its directive at column 0, so the second loop was never at risk.</evidence>
<parameter name="impact">`./install` runs this generator, and a non-zero exit from a step that "only regenerates docs" is the kind of failure that gets normalised — the completions, `local/md/` docs and manpages for the other 90 specs were all written correctly, so the run looked cosmetically fine while reporting failure. The five KDL parse dumps drown the real log. Any future doc file under `local/bin/` that names the directive reintroduces it, and each one adds five more warnings and a further increment to the exit status.</impact>
<parameter name="fix">Anchor the selector to column 0, matching `usage`'s own requirement and the two greps the dfm assembly step in the same file already uses:

```sh
for spec in "$DOTFILES"/local/bin/*; do
  [[ -f "$spec" ]] || continue
  # Anchored at column 0, matching the dfm assembly step below and `usage`
  # itself, which only extracts directives that start the line. An unanchored
  # match also selects prose: local/bin/CLAUDE.md documents the convention and
  # writes `#USAGE` inline, so it was handed to `usage`, failed to parse as
  # KDL five times over, and took the generator's exit status to 4.
  grep -qE '^(#USAGE|//USAGE)' "$spec" 2> /dev/null || continue
```

Verify the count moves by exactly one and the status clears:

```
DOTFILES="$PWD" bash scripts/install-completions.sh; echo "rc=$?"
```

Expect `Done: processed 90 specs (0 warnings)` and `rc=0`. Confirm `dfm` still generates — it is the assembled spec and the one most likely to break — with `grep -c 'Generating for: dfm$'`.

Note that `local/md/` and `local/man/man1/*.1` are gitignored (`.gitignore:95-96`), so a regression here shows up only in the generator's exit status, never as a diff. That is the argument for keeping the exit status meaningful.</fix>

No stale local/md/CLAUDE.md or local/man/man1/CLAUDE.1 were left by the earlier failing runs. shellcheck -x, shfmt and `yarn lint` (rc=0) all clean; generated output is byte-identical to before, and since local/md/ and local/man/man1/*.1 are gitignored the only tracked change is the one line in the generator.
